newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu learning the hard way.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu learning the hard way.

text.p: There's no smoking gun. There are no Oval Office tapes. But that hasn't stopped Israelis from likening the political woes of their prime minister Benjamin (Bibi) Netanyahu to Watergate.
"Bibigate" has been running almost nightly on the television news for more than a month now.
The script's a little thin. The reporter who broke the story has not produced hard evidence linking Netanyahu to her allegations of political corruption in his Likud-led coalition government.
But the episodes that had the leader of the Middle East's superpower hiring a criminal lawyer and being questioned for four hours "under caution" by police, had the chattering classes enthralled.

Police are questioning senior government officials and say they may interview Netanyahu again. The material for what journalists say is turning into a mini-series comes largely from police leaks which the government is furiously trying to plug.

Based on what they have seen so far political commentators and Western diplomats do not believe that Netanyahu is in serious danger of following U.S. president Richard Nixon into the political sunset.

"The attempt to create some sort of psychopolitical or historiopolitical comparison with another culture isn't a serious thing," Netanyahu told Israel Radio on Tuesday when asked about the comparison to Nixon, who resigned in 1974.

But some say the affair has shown the 47-year-old ex-commando to be inexperienced, surrounded by poor advisers and misguided by his suspicion of the political and security establishment which is dominated by the opposition Labour party.
Netanyahu, whose first time at the cabinet table was as prime minister, is under fire for naming a Likud insider and non-establishment figure, Roni Bar-On, as attorney-general in late January.
TV ALLEGES SHADY DEAL OVER HEBRON
Bar-On quit only 12 hours into the job amid uproar about his suitability.
Then, Channel One Television pointed to an even darker cloud on Netanyahu's dawning career as an international peacemaker.
It alleged that his government's belated approval of the Hebron peace deal with the Palestinians, which enhanced Netanyahu's stock in Western capitals, was mired in sleaze.

The television said Aryeh Deri, the rising star of Israel's Oriental Jewish community and a pillar of Netanyahu's fractious coalition, gave his Shas party's support to Hebron in return for Bar-On's appointment. Deri, on trial for the past three years for corruption, expected Bar-On to arrange a plea bargain.
Netanyahu, Deri and Bar-On have denied any wrongdoing. Netanyahu has ordered an inquiry into the allegations.
Even if there is no fire, the smoke from this scandal continues to swirl around the prime minister's office, obscuring what Netanyahu supporters believe to be his progress on the peace front.
After a string of blunders following his election triumph last May, Netanyahu had begun to repair the damage at home.
By withdrawing Israeli troops from Hebron he put relations with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat back on track, much to the relief of peace-sponsor President Bill Clinton.
His handling over the past two weeks of the controversial policy of building Jewish settlements in Arab East Jerusalem shows he has learnt that timing and presentation are crucial, commentators say.

Last September, spurning army and secret service warnings in favour of the promptings of right-wing politicians and financiers, Netanyahu opened a tunnel entrance near a Moslem shrine in Jerusalem. The storm that followed killed 61 Palestinians, 15 Israeli soldiers and almost scuppered the peace process.
This time, Likud officials believe Netanyahu has almost pulled off the latest attempt to consolidate Israel's hold on East Jerusalem.
NETANYAHU'S LEARNING CURVE

"He's learning on the job," said Hirsh Goodman, editor of the Jerusalem Report magazine. For a leader who inherited the straightjacket of Labour's peace policy, and who has to hold together a coalition ranging from secular Russians to Zionist settlers and ultra-Orthodox rabbis, Netanyahu is not doing so badly, Goodman admits grudgingly.

He is moving Likud to the centre and positioning himself to face off against Ehud Barak, a former army chief who is frontrunner to replace Shimon Peres as Labour party leader, in the election in the year 2000.
"He's going to go into the election saying he has delivered peace with security," says Goodman, pointing to political pragmatism rather than deeply held beliefs as Netanyahu's driving force.
Critics say that Netanyahu is shallow, impetuous and swayed by a group of inexperienced political advisers.
They credit Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, a political novice who has only just hung up his general's uniform, with curbing some of the government's wilder impulses.

"The fact that Netanyahu is an outsider and the fact that he doesn't trust anyone in the Isareli establishment leads him to fight against this establishment and in the process reach wrong decisions," said political commentator Chemi Shalev.
The appointment of Bar-On is a case in point, Shalev said.

Likud supporters believe Netanyahu will have to change his inner circle once the Bar-On affair dies down. If the investigation clears Netanyahu of accusations of criminal breach of trust but does not completely exonerate him "all hell will break loose", Shalev said.
